title: Richa Chadha on 'Musafiri': Bollywood 'Needs Restructuring, So It's Not Such a Big Game of Chance'
excerpt: The actor's YouTube travel series explores Mumbai's disappearing corners — and doubles as her first outing as director and writer, 18 years after her debut.
body:
• Richa Chadha's eight-episode travel series Musafiri launched on YouTube on September 25, exploring Mumbai's lesser-known corners — from its mangroves to its disappearing Bandra bungalows.
  • Chadha told The Hollywood Reporter India she chose YouTube over streamers for "even more creative control" — and because "education should be free."
  • The actor, who became a mother in 2024, says the industry "needs some (re)structuring, so that it's not such a big game of chance" — and that "not all actors are interested only in their careers."
  • Musafiri marks 18 years since her debut in Oye Lucky! Lucky Oye! and her first outing as a director and debut writer.

Richa Chadha has played gangsters' wives, lawyers and courtesans — but her latest role is behind the camera. The actor's first travel series, Musafiri, premiered on YouTube on September 25, an eight-episode exploration of Mumbai's history, communities and vanishing corners. And in a new interview with The Hollywood Reporter India, Chadha used the launch to make a broader case: Bollywood itself needs restructuring.

"I think the industry needs some (re)structuring, so that it's not such a big game of chance."

— Richa Chadha, to The Hollywood Reporter India

Why YouTube, not a streamer

Chadha told Variety India that YouTube was a deliberate choice. "I wanted even more creative control than I previously had with being a producer," she said. "I don't want to listen to some executives telling me about what will work and what will not work... Secondly, I wanted to make an educational show and education should be free. That's my opinion. That's why I didn't want to put it on a platform that has a subscription model, and it is on YouTube. You can watch it in Ireland, Pakistan or Kenya."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=oh8vDRJaPaE https://x.com/Arun_Kaku05/status/2106229237657350554

The series began as a festival-centred idea but expanded, she told Bollywood Hungama, when she realised "there are a lot of topics to cover" — from 65-million-year-old Gilbert Hill in Andheri to the dhol players of Lalbaugcha Raja who come from different communities. What started as a years-long research document became an eight-episode love letter to the city that shaped her.

Motherhood, and a changed lens

Chadha became a mother in 2024, and she describes a "perspective shift" since. "You start documenting things you think are fast disappearing, like the mangroves of Mumbai or the quaint little bungalows in Bandra," she told The Hollywood Reporter India. "You also start wondering things like whether your daughter will be able to read books when she grows up."

For Chadha, Musafiri is also about something structural: women's access to public space. "When I started working on this, there were no women trying to reclaim public spaces," she said. "We should be able to move around freely and see our own city, at night and during the day."

"Not all actors are interested only in their careers"

Asked what pushed her to take the directorial reins, Chadha was characteristically direct: "I just have a different kind of interest. Not all actors are interested only in their own careers. Some like pottery, some like photography, and I like history." She is adamant it changes nothing about her acting — "It remains the same, and I'm just adding a new dimension."

This year marks 18 since her 2006 debut in Oye Lucky! Lucky Oye!, and two since her last screen appearance in Sanjay Leela Bhansali's Heeramandi. Her verdict on where Hindi cinema stands after the COVID-era losses: "I think it needs a better conversation around crises and lingering issues."

Context: an industry in flux

Chadha's critique lands at a moment when Bollywood's economics are visibly shifting. Her husband Ali Fazal's Mirzapur The Movie recently crossed Rs. 200 crore domestically — a milestone she celebrated as proof that "outsiders" can anchor big-budget films without the industry's usual handful of bankable stars. Her longer-running argument, made earlier this year, is that indie cinema must cast on authenticity rather than chasing the nod of "5 top male actors" for commercial cover.

What's next

Chadha plans to take Musafiri beyond Mumbai and across India eventually. Whether her call for industry restructuring gets a hearing will be measured in the films that get made — and the ones that don't have to wait on a star's calendar.
